rv.q: In a world that often seems far from those values, Herzog's play shines like a candle in the dark.
Where we all ended up was a revelation.
It’s McAdams, with her fetching warmth, who alters the temperature.
That gesture is typical of the understated yet gutting quality of this production of Mary Jane, which cuts the quotidian open to get to the bone of the existential.
Rachel McAdams gives a performance of such emotional authenticity and raw power that you feel as if you're witnessing something deeply private and profound.
There are two sick people in Mary Jane's home, we realize, and Herzog has coaxed us into falling in love with both of them. The realization, just like the play, is gutting.
Herzog's skill as a writer means that you feel the conversation alongside McAdams' character, you are alongside her on a journey no one wants to take.
Healthcare is a vast ecosystem of treatment, suffering and healing, of hospitals, bills and logistics.
“Mary Jane” stays with viewers long after they leave the theater.
Rachel McAdams gives a powerhouse performance as a single mother caring for her chronically ill son in this emotionally devastating Broadway drama.
The only reason I got through this astoundingly over-praised travesty is Rachel McAdams.
Her Mary Jane has inscribed another notch on my heart.

When Alex has a seizure midway through the play, the mounting dread and panicked 911 call are distressingly familiar. So, too, is the purgatory-like state of the hospital waiting room, which is brilliantly conveyed through Ben Stanton’s stark lighting and Lael Jellinek’s deceptively simple scenic design.
Mary Jane is a beautiful, emotional story providing an intimate portrait of a caregiving mother trying to get by.
I left the theater full of gratitude, both for my own blessings and for the beauty and generosity that make “Mary Jane” such a difficult and life-affirming work.
Anne Kaufman, repeating her staging from the play’s earlier NYC incarnation at Theatre Workshop, has delivered a beautifully calibrated production that expertly mines its subtleties.
McAdams winds up startlingly effective in a play whose weight and power sneak up on you.
Herzog has written a mournful lullaby, somehow simultaneously upsetting and soothing, thoughtful and gut-wrenching.
Her Mary Jane – a triumph, if one that points to better stage outings to come – is no different.
Mary Jane allows us to perceive how community affects motherhood.
What might have been a tearjerker is so much more, a chance to completely belong in this character’s mind and heart.
Stoic is not an easy look to convey to an audience, and McAdams’ performance doesn’t really take shape until Mary Jane sets up residence in the hospital.

Nonetheless, Herzog leaves us with a delicate understanding that, whether we are the mother of a sick child, a struggling college student or an overworked hospital employee, life is what we choose to make of it.
Despite a plethora of outstanding performances, consider this a trigger warning.
Mary Jane is unfussy naturalism that sneaks up on you with a pregnant power.
Most importantly, it ought to be enjoyed for its melancholy, authenticity, and simplicity, especially since there are moments where Rachel McAdams will break your heart.
The show is a phenomenal window into the world of caregiving.

cn.t: Herzog's intimate drama about a mother caring for her severely ill son earns praise for its understated authenticity and McAdams' powerhouse Broadway debut, though some find it too muted to fully land its emotional impact.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).

Headout and SeatPlan both flag rows E-J as the best price-to-sightline ratio: meaningfully cheaper than the A-D premium band while staying close in a 634-seat room. Slight orchestra rake keeps sightlines clean. Mezzanine overhang (per SeatPlan) begins at row G but the intimate room means no sound-deadening issue in this band.

sg.vl: Under the overhang but still engaged
sg.ra: SeatPlan confirms the Mezzanine overhangs from row G back, so K-Q sit fully under. The room is small enough (Headout: 'one of Broadway's more intimate spaces') that rear orchestra remains engaged. Rows P and Q are accessibility-friendly (no aisle stairs per folliesbroadway). Legroom tightens beyond row O per SeatPlan.

Headout and SeatPlan both name AA-BB center as premier seats with 'clean, direct look at the stage' and elevation that improves the view. aviewfrommyseat user on Mezzanine L row A aisle reported 'lots of legroom' with only a thin safety bar as minor issue. Excellent rake across the mezzanine.

SeatPlan and Headout both emphasize that the mezzanine has 'excellent rake' keeping all rows elevated with clean sightlines; Headout says 'no truly bad seat in the house'. Small 224-seat mezzanine means even row G stays close. Row F offers transfer seats and row E has wheelchair spaces (Headout accessibility).

vr.q: Rachel McAdams is amazing in the titular role. The selflessness Mary Jane brings to the way she cares for her child is similar to the selflessness Rachel McAdams brings to caring for the text.
overall I think this play is worth seeing because it's tackling a subject matter that's important and it's tackling it in a very thoughtful intelligent way
Ultimately, because of the subject matter, this really wasn't a show for me. But I am really glad I saw it. There's a lot of really good parts to it.
